newsitem.title: HONG KONG: London fighting shy of HK commitments - legislator.
newsitem.headline: London fighting shy of HK commitments - legislator.

text.p: British government leaders have refused to make concrete commitments to tackle pressing problems facing Hong Kong when China takes it back next year, a leading politician in the colony said on Thursday.

Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's Democratic Party, has just returned from a lobbying mission to London to persuade British government leaders to raise the question of China's plan to disband the territory's elected legislature.
Lee made the trip just before Britain's House of Commons holds what may be its last debate on Hong Kong.
Britain hands Hong Kong back to China on July 1, 1997, ending a century and a half of colonial rule.
China has promised Hong Kong a high degree of self-rule for the next 50 years under the Sino-British Joint Declaration.
But nerves have turned jittery since Beijing vowed to replace the elected legislature with an appointed provisional legislature which will be formed next month.
Lee hinted that London, while sympathetic over the imminent dismantling of Hong Kong's elected chamber, was cautious about confronting Beijing.
"The government ministers were concerned, they don't like the provisional legislature, but they will not say it is in breach of the Joint Declaration," Lee told Reuters.

"What I wanted to do was to get the British government to say during the debate that the setting up of the appointed legislature is in breach of the Joint Declaration," he said. "I'm afraid the indications are they would not say it."
Lee said the British ministers he met included Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and Home Secretary Michael Howard.

In Hong Kong, more than a dozen pro-democracy activists prepared to greet visiting Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen by staging a 30-hour hunger strike and sit-in to protest against the setting up of the provisional legislature.
Qian, on his first official trip to the colony, was due to arrive at the Hong Kong Convention Centre on Friday morning to anoint a 400-strong Selection Committee.
Newly-formed under Beijing's tight reins, the committee will choose Hong Kong's first post-handover Chief Executive and form the 60-member provisional legislature.
